figures.cap: cross-section of pipe with water of width 20 cm and depth d

parts.latex:
A cylindrical pipe with a radius of 12.5 cm is filled with water to a depth, $d$ cm, as shown.

The surface of the water has a width of 20 cm.

\exfigure{300_q12_1}

What is the depth of water in the pipe?

solutions.latex:
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so the half-width of the water surface is $10$ cm.

Let $h$ be the distance from the centre to the surface. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $12.5$ (the radius), Pythagoras' theorem gives
$$\begin{aligned} h^2 + 10^2 &= 12.5^2\\ h^2 &= 156.25 - 100 = 56.25\\ h &= 7.5 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
From the figure the centre is above the water surface, so the depth is the radius minus $h$:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 12.5 - 7.5\\ &= 5.0 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

meta.generated_note: MCQ working written from answer key B.

Round 1 had a \halo typo that stopped the compile, so round 2 is the only rendered version. The redraw score is held down only by where the stipple dots fall (rule 5). Rules 1, 3, 4, 5, 5b, 6a, 11.

figures.cap: park with lake and grassed section

parts.latex: Using two applications of the trapezoidal rule, calculate the approximate area of the grassed section.
Hence calculate the approximate area of the lake, to the nearest square metre.

solutions.latex:
The grassed section has parallel sides 160, 150 and 250 with strip width 100, so apply the trapezoidal rule twice.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 100\times(160+150) + \dfrac{1}{2}\times 100\times(150+250) \\ &= 50\times 310 + 50\times 400 \\ &= 35\,500 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total area of the park is the rectangle plus the semicircle.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total area} &= 200\times 250 + \dfrac{1}{2}\times\pi\times 100^2 \\ &= 65\,707.96\ldots \\ &\approx 65\,708 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The lake is the total area less the grassed section.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lake area} &= 65\,708 - 35\,500 \\ &= 30\,208 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the rectangle and semicircle, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: cylinder on a hemisphere

solutions.latex:
The hemisphere has radius $3$ cm and the cylinder radius $2$ cm. The surface consists of five pieces.

Curved surface of the hemisphere, half of $4\pi r^2$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\pi\times 3^2$$
Exposed flat top of the hemisphere (an annulus):
$$\pi\times 3^2 - \pi\times 2^2$$
Top of the cylinder:
$$\pi\times 2^2$$
Curved side of the cylinder:
$$2\pi\times 2\times 3$$
Adding these:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\pi\times 3^2 + \pi\times 3^2 - \pi\times 2^2 + \pi\times 2^2 + 2\pi\times 6 \\ &\approx 122.5 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates the curved area of the cylinder AND of the hemisphere
Calculates the curved area of the cylinder OR of the hemisphere

271_q34_1.notes: Drew the cylinder on the hemisphere. Hidden edges are dashed (aux): the back of the cylinder base, and the back rim of the hemisphere behind the cylinder. The 4 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm dimension lines are dashed with end bars and filled -latex heads (rule 4). As in the crop, each label sits in a gap in its dimension line. NOT TO SCALE is kept.

figures.cap: triangular prism on top of a cube

solutions.latex:
The triangular face has height equal to the total height minus the cube's side:
$$11 - 8 = 3 \text{ cm}$$
Five square faces:
$$8^2 \times 5 = 320$$
Two triangular faces:
$$\dfrac{3 \times 8}{2} \times 2 = 24$$
Two rectangular faces:
$$5 \times 8 \times 2 = 80$$
Total surface area:
$$\begin{aligned} SA &= 320 + 24 + 80 \\ &= 424 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates the area of two different relevant faces, or equivalent merit
Calculates the area of one relevant face, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: open rectangular box 2 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm

parts.latex:
What is the external surface area of the following open box?

\exfigure{16_q1_1}

solutions.latex:
The box is open, so it has a base and four sides but no top.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Base} &= 5\times 2 = 10 \text{ cm}^2 \\ \text{Two long sides} &= 2\times(5\times 3) = 30 \text{ cm}^2 \\ \text{Two short ends} &= 2\times(2\times 3) = 12 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Surface area} &= 10+30+12 \\ &= 52 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is A.

$$\begin{aligned} l &= \dfrac{175}{360} \times 2\pi \times 8.1 \\ &\approx 24.74 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 24.74 + 8.1 + 8.1 \\ &= 40.94 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: hemispherical tank, radius 2 m

parts.latex:
The volume, $V$, of a sphere is given by the formula

$$V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3,$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

A tank consists of the bottom half of a sphere of radius 2 metres, as shown.

\exfigure{38_q16_1}

Find the volume of the tank in cubic metres, correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
The tank is half a sphere, so use half of the given formula with $r=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\times\pi\times 2^3 \\ &\approx 16.8 \text{ m}^3 \text{ (one decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ V \approx 16.8 \text{ m}^3$$
criteria: Attempts to use $V=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, or equivalent merit

38_q16_1.notes: Hemispherical tank: an elliptical rim with a half-ellipse bowl at the crop's size. Centre dot, and two filled-arrow pieces either side of the '2 m' label going from the centre to the rim. Rules 1, 3, 4.

figures.cap: capsule container with three soccer balls, diameter 23 cm

parts.latex:
A container for soccer balls is made using two half spheres joined to each end of a cylindrical body.

\exfigure{40_q34_1}

Three soccer balls fit exactly inside the container. Each ball has a diameter of 23 cm.

The hemispherical ends of the container just touch the surface of the soccer balls.

What is the total surface area of the container? Give your answer in square metres correct to 1 decimal place.

solutions.latex:
The container is a sphere's surface (two hemispheres, radius $\dfrac{23}{2}$ cm) plus the curved surface of a cylinder of the same radius and length $2\times 23=46$ cm (two balls).

$$\text{Surface area of sphere}=4\pi\left(\dfrac{23}{2}\right)^2$$

$$\text{Curved surface of cylinder}=2\pi\times\dfrac{23}{2}\times(23\times 2)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \text{Total surface area} &= 4\pi\left(\dfrac{23}{2}\right)^2+2\pi\times\dfrac{23}{2}\times 46 \\ &= 4985.707\ldots \text{ cm}^2 \\ &\approx 4985.7 \text{ cm}^2 \\ &\approx 0.5 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The total surface area is $0.5 \text{ m}^2$ (1 decimal place).
criteria: Finds the total surface area, or equivalent merit
Finds the surface area of the cylinder or sphere, or equivalent merit
Attempts to find the surface area of a sphere, or equivalent merit

Not redrawn as a line diagram (rule 8): keep the original crop. If a line drawing is wanted later: capsule outline, three tangent circles, seam lines at the hemisphere joins, and a 23 cm dimension arrow.

parts.latex:
Which of the following shapes has a perimeter of 12 cm?

NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is the sum of all the side lengths. Check each shape.

A: opposite sides of the rectangle are equal (marked), so the sides are $2, 4, 2, 4$.
$$P = 2+4+2+4 = 12 \text{ cm}$$
B: $P = 4+2+3 = 9 \text{ cm}$.

C: all four sides are equal (marked), so $P = 4\times 4 = 16 \text{ cm}$.

D: the two slanted sides are equal (marked), so $P = 1+4+1+5 = 11 \text{ cm}$.

Only shape A has a perimeter of 12 cm, so the answer is option A.

figures.cap: tub with ten cylinders in two rows of five

parts.latex:
A rectangular tub has length 50 cm, width 20 cm and unknown height ($h$).

Ten identical cylinders are arranged inside the tub in two rows of five.

Each cylinder has diameter 10 cm and height $h$ cm.

Exactly 3 litres of water is poured into the tub to fill all the spaces around the cylinders.

\exfigure{5836_q33_1}

What is the height of the tub, correct to the nearest whole number?

solutions.latex:
The water fills the cross-section not occupied by the cylinders, over height $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= (20 \times 50) - (10 \times \pi \times 5^2) \\ &= 214.6018\ldots \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $3\text{ L} = 3000\text{ cm}^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= A \times h \\ 3000 &= 214.6018\ldots \times h \\ h &= 13.979\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h \approx 14 \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Finds the total volume of the empty space, or equivalent merit
Finds one relevant volume in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit
Finds one relevant area, or equivalent merit

6009.stem:
A toy has a curved surface on the top which has been shaded as shown. The toy has a uniform cross-section and a rectangular base.

\exfigure{5834_q26_1}

figures.cap: prism-shaped toy with curved top surface (NOT TO SCALE)

parts.latex: Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to find an approximate area of the cross-section of the toy.

The total surface area of the plastic toy is $1300\text{ cm}^2$.

What is the approximate area of the curved surface?

The measurements shown on the diagram are given to the nearest millimetre.

What is the percentage error of the measurement of 10.2 cm? Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.note: Percentage error of a measurement (measurement error) is not in the 2024 course.

solutions.latex:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule, with strip width $5.1$ cm and heights $6$, $3.8$ and $0$ cm:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{5.1}{2}(6 + 3.8) + \dfrac{5.1}{2}(3.8 + 0) \\ &\approx 34.68 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use 2 applications of the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total surface area is the two cross-sections, the rectangular faces and the curved surface.
$$\begin{aligned} 1300 &= (2 \times 34.68) + (10.2 \times 40) + (6 \times 40) + \text{curved surface} \\ 1300 &= 717.36 + \text{curved surface} \\ \text{curved surface} &= 1300 - 717.36 \\ &= 582.64 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds at least 2 correct areas as part of a surface area calculation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The absolute error is half the measuring unit.
$$\text{Absolute error} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.1 = 0.05 \text{ cm}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage error} &= \dfrac{0.05}{10.2} \times 100\% \\ &= 0.4901\ldots\% \\ &= 0.490\% \text{ (3 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides correct absolute error, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: square-based pyramid containing spheres (NOT TO SCALE)

parts.latex:
Solid spheres are placed inside a square-based pyramid as shown.

\exfigure{5834_q32_1}

The base of the pyramid has side lengths of 14 cm. The height of the pyramid is $h$ cm. The radius of each sphere is 1.5 cm.

The amount of empty space remaining inside the pyramid after 30 spheres have been placed inside the pyramid is $634\text{ cm}^3$.

What is the height, $h$, of the pyramid? Give your answer correct to the nearest centimetre.

solutions.latex:
The volume of 30 spheres is
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 1.5^3 \times 30 \\ &= 424.115\ldots \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
The pyramid volume is the volume of the spheres plus the empty space:
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{pyramid}} &= 424.115\ldots + 634 \\ &= 1058.115\ldots \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
Using $V = \dfrac{1}{3}Ah$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1058.115 &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times (14 \times 14) \times h \\ h &= \dfrac{1058.115 \times 3}{14 \times 14} \\ &\approx 16.2 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h = 16 \text{ cm (to the nearest whole number)}$$
criteria: Provides evidence of equating volumes to find $h$, or equivalent merit
Finds the volume of a sphere, or equivalent merit

6128.stem:
A tunnel connecting two cities is to be built in the shape of an annulus as shown in the diagram below. The tunnel is to be made from concrete and the curved surface is to be covered with plants to make it more environmentally friendly.

\exfigure{497_q36_1}

figures.cap: tunnel with outer width 50 m, inner width 30 m, length 12 km

parts.latex: What is the volume of concrete needed to make the tunnel, to the nearest cubic metre?

The landscape architect needs to know the area to be covered by the plants.

Calculate the surface area of the outer tunnel to be covered. Give your answer correct to the nearest square metre.

solutions.latex:
The tunnel is half an annulus-shaped cylinder: the volume is half the difference of two cylinders of length $12\,000$ m (outer radius $25$, inner radius $15$).
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{\pi \times 25^2 \times 12\,000}{2} - \dfrac{\pi \times 15^2 \times 12\,000}{2} \\ &\approx 7\,539\,822 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one cylinder volume, or equivalent merit
Uses a correct volume formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Radii and length taken from the source working.

solutions.latex:
The curved surface is half the lateral area of the outer cylinder.
$$\begin{aligned} SA &= \dfrac{2\pi \times 25 \times 12\,000}{2} \\ &\approx 942\,478 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses a correct curved surface area formula, or equivalent merit

solution sketch: field diagram in guidelines (different version of Q23) with 58 degree angle marked

parts.latex: Calculate the area of the subdivision to the nearest square metre.

The developer needs at least 550 square metres for each section of the subdivision. Also, the local council needs 10% of the land for the required infrastructure.

What is the maximum number of sections the developer could make from his land development?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{719_q23_s1}

The angles at $O$ between neighbouring rays are the differences of the bearings:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle AOB &= 360^\circ-316^\circ+58^\circ = 102^\circ \\ \angle BOC &= 125^\circ-58^\circ = 67^\circ \\ \angle COD &= 238^\circ-125^\circ = 113^\circ \\ \angle DOA &= 316^\circ-238^\circ = 78^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Using $A=\dfrac12ab\sin C$ for each triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac12(84)(57)\sin102^\circ+\dfrac12(57)(62)\sin67^\circ+\dfrac12(62)(77)\sin113^\circ+\dfrac12(77)(84)\sin78^\circ \\ &= 2341.68\ldots+1626.53\ldots+2197.24\ldots+3163.32\ldots \\ &= 9328.79\ldots \\ &\approx 9329 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle AOB$ and substitutes into the area formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Source drawing kept.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the school worked another version of the question (area of triangle $AOB$ only, $2342$ m$^2$); the subdivision is all four triangles, $9329$ m$^2$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the school worked another version of the question (area of triangle $AOB$ only, $2342$ m$^2$); the subdivision is all four triangles, $9329$ m$^2$.

solutions.latex:
The council takes $10\%$, leaving $90\%$ of the land.
$$0.90 \times 9329 = 8396.1 \text{ m}^2$$
$$\dfrac{8396.1}{550} = 15.26\ldots$$
Only whole sections of at least $550 \text{ m}^2$ count, so round down.
$$\therefore\ 15 \text{ sections}$$

figures.cap: capsule: cylinder with hemispherical ends, length 18 cm, diameter 6 cm, partly filled with water

parts.latex:
A capsule of length 18 cm and diameter 6 cm is formed by joining an open hemisphere at each end of an open cylinder, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{500_q10_1}

Water is poured into the capsule and fills one third of its volume.

Calculate the volume of water in the capsule, correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The radius is $3$ cm, so the cylinder length is $18-6=12$ cm.

The two hemispheres make one sphere, so the capsule volume is that of a sphere plus a cylinder.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3+\pi r^2 h \\ &= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\times 3^3+\pi\times 3^2\times 12 \\ &= 36\pi + 108\pi = 144\pi \\ &\approx 452.389 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
The water fills one third of this.
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{water}} &= \dfrac{1}{3}\times 452.389 \\ &\approx 150.80 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: park: rectangle with semicircle, lake and grassed section with measurements

parts.latex: Using two applications of the trapezoidal rule, calculate the approximate area of the grassed section.
Hence, calculate the approximate area of the lake, to the nearest square metre.

solutions.latex:
The grassed section has width 100 m per strip, with parallel sides $160, 150$ and $150, 250$.

Applying the trapezoidal rule to each strip:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\times 100\times(160+150)+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 100\times(150+250) \\ &= 50\times 310+50\times 400 \\ &= 35\,500 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total area of the park is the rectangle plus the semicircle.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{total}} &= 200\times 250+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\pi\times 100^2 \\ &\approx 65\,708 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The lake is the total area less the grassed section.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{lake}} &= 65\,708-35\,500 \\ &= 30\,208 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the rectangle and semicircle, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Two trapezoidal rule applications, each with width $110$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{20+90}{2}\times 110+\dfrac{90+150}{2}\times 110 \\ &= 6050+13\,200 \\ &= 19\,250 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Volume with average depth $50$ m:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 19\,250\times 50 \\ &= 962\,500 \text{ m}^3 \\ &= 962\,500 \text{ kL} \end{aligned}$$
Since $1 \text{ ML}=1000 \text{ kL}$:
$$962\,500\div 1000=962.5 \text{ ML}$$
criteria: Finds the volume, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule, find an estimate for the area of the irregular shape shown below. (Each square on the grid is one square unit.)

solutions.latex:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule on $0\le x\le 4$ give strip width
$$h=\dfrac{4-0}{2}=2$$
so the function values are read at $x=0,\,2,\,4$ from the grid: $2$, $4$ and $3$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\big(y_0+2y_1+y_2\big) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{2}\big(2+2\times 4+3\big) \\ &= 13 \text{ square units} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

figures.cap: cheese wedge, height 15 cm
sector cross section, radius 18 cm, angle 40 degrees, arc length l

solutions.latex:
The cross-section is a sector of radius $18$ cm and angle $40^\circ$, and $l$ is its arc length.
$$\begin{aligned} l &= \dfrac{40}{360}\times 2\pi\times 18 \\ &= 4\pi \\ &\approx 12.57 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
The wedge has two sector faces, a curved face and two rectangular faces of height $15$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sector faces: } 2\times \dfrac{40}{360}\times \pi\times 18^2 &= 72\pi \\ \text{Curved face: } l\times 15 &= 60\pi \\ \text{Rectangular faces: } 2\times 18\times 15 &= 540 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Surface area} &= 72\pi + 60\pi + 540 \\ &= 132\pi + 540 \\ &\approx 954.7 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ l \approx 12.57 \text{ cm and surface area} \approx 954.7 \text{ cm}^2$$
criteria: Finds $l$ and the areas of most of the faces, or equivalent merit

meta.generated_note: Assumes the wedge's flat rectangular faces are the two radii (18 cm) by 15 cm, as in the figure.

figures.cap: cylinder containing three tennis balls

solutions.latex:
Each ball has radius $r$, so the cylinder has radius $r$. Three balls touch in a column, so the cylinder's height is $3\times 2r=6r$.

The volume of the cylinder is
$$V_{\text{cyl}}=\pi r^2\times 6r=6\pi r^3$$
The volume of the three balls is
$$V_{\text{balls}}=3\times\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3=4\pi r^3$$
The fraction occupied is
$$\dfrac{4\pi r^3}{6\pi r^3}=\dfrac{2}{3}$$

6419.stem:
Consider the composite figure that is made of a right-angled triangle and a rectangle.

\exfigure{717_q20_1}

figures.cap: composite figure of right-angled triangle and rectangle

parts.latex: Calculate the value of $h$.
Calculate the area of the composite figure.

solutions.latex:
By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2&=13^2-12^2\\&=25\end{aligned}$$
$$x=5$$
$$\begin{aligned}h&=11+5\\&=16\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

The area is the triangle plus the rectangle.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=A_1+A_2\\&=\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 12\times 5\right)+(12\times 11)\\&=162\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the triangle or the rectangle, or equivalent merit

Dimension lines (13 m along the slope, 11 m, h, 12 m with end bars) use fine aux dashes and filled Latex heads, broken around their labels instead of using white halos (transparent background). The 13 m label is rotated along the slope. NOT TO SCALE is placed as in the crop. Remaining colour is the scan's long dashes and open chevrons, which house style replaces. Rules 3, 4, 5c, 6a, 11.

solutions.latex:
Two strips share the width 45 cm, so each strip has width $h=\dfrac{45}{2}=22.5$ cm.

Applying the trapezoidal rule to each strip:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{22.5}{2}(15+10)+\dfrac{22.5}{2}(10+8) \\ &= 483.75 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The volume is the area times the thickness.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 483.75\times 4 \\ &= 1935 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: front view of concrete wall with heights 15, 25, 20, 26, 14 m over 48 m

parts.latex: Using four applications of the trapezoidal rule, estimate the area of the concrete wall.

The concrete wall will have a thickness of 28 m.

Calculate the volume of concrete required to build the wall, correct to the nearest cubic metre.

solutions.latex:
Divide the wall into four sections of width 12 m, with areas $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$. Using the trapezoidal rule, $A = \dfrac{h}{2}(d_f + d_l)$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= \dfrac{12}{2} \times (15 + 25) = 240 \text{ m}^2 \\ A_2 &= \dfrac{12}{2} \times (25 + 20) = 270 \text{ m}^2 \\ A_3 &= \dfrac{12}{2} \times (20 + 26) = 276 \text{ m}^2 \\ A_4 &= \dfrac{12}{2} \times (26 + 14) = 240 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total area} &= 240 + 270 + 276 + 240 \\ &= 1026 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates the area of the wall with one error

solutions.latex:
The volume is the area of the wall times its thickness.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 1026 \times 28 \\ &= 28\,728 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

The crop's open chevron heads are replaced with filled Latex heads (rule 4) and its long dashes with the house aux dash (rule 3). NOT TO SCALE kept.
